title: Connecticut v. Doehr
lead: An assault plaintiff encumbers the defendant’s home before notice, using a short affidavit. The homeowner’s challenge turns on the risk of deciding a disputed fight from one side’s account.

actors.name: John F. DiGiovanni
actors.role: Assault-and-battery plaintiff who obtained the attachment.

actors.name: Brian K. Doehr
actors.role: Owner of the attached Meriden home; brought the federal due-process challenge.

actors.name: State of Connecticut
actors.role: Intervened on appeal to defend its attachment statute; Supreme Court petitioner with DiGiovanni.

proceedings: The Connecticut Superior Court authorized a $75,000 attachment on March 17, 1988.
Doehr sued federally; the district court upheld the statute and granted DiGiovanni summary judgment.
A divided Second Circuit reversed in Pinsky v. Duncan, 898 F.2d 852 (1990).
The Supreme Court unanimously affirmed the judgment and remanded on June 6, 1991; only four Justices supported the separate bond rule.
limits: The source-brief transformation states the 1991 as-applied decision, without a new audit or present-law certification. The assault allegations were not adjudicated as facts in this constitutional case. Part IV’s bond requirement was a four-Justice plurality, and the state-statute appendix did not certify the constitutionality of every surveyed procedure.

review.basis: Fresh comparison with complete effective canonical brief; no new independent full-opinion audit claimed.

sections.title: DiGiovanni seeks security for a future assault judgment
sections.cue: What connection did the claimant have to Doehr’s home?
paragraphs: John F. DiGiovanni alleged that Brian K. Doehr had willfully, wantonly and maliciously assaulted him. He planned an assault-and-battery suit and wanted Doehr’s assets available if he eventually won damages. On March 15, 1988, he applied in Connecticut Superior Court for a $75,000 attachment of Doehr’s home in Meriden. The alleged fight did not concern the home, and DiGiovanni had no pre-existing interest in it or in Doehr’s other property.

Connecticut law allowed a judge to authorize attachment of real property without an advance hearing upon a sworn showing of probable cause to sustain the claim. It required no plaintiff’s bond to cover harm from a wrongful attachment. DiGiovanni supplied five one-sentence affidavit paragraphs: the complaint was true; Doehr had willfully, wantonly and maliciously assaulted him; the assault had broken his left wrist, bruised his right eye and caused other injuries; he had medical expenses; and in his opinion those facts established probable cause for a favorable judgment. These were his assertions, not a determination of the contested fight.

On March 17, a judge found probable cause on the submissions and ordered attachment up to $75,000. The sheriff attached the home four days later. Doehr received notice only afterward, before he had even been served with the tort complaint. The notice explained that he could request a hearing to dispute probable cause, seek modification or vacation, substitute a bond, or assert an exemption.

sections.title: Doehr challenges the procedure in federal court
sections.cue: What did the two lower federal courts decide?
paragraphs: Doehr did not request the offered post-attachment hearing. He instead sued DiGiovanni in federal district court, seeking a declaration that the statute violated Fourteenth Amendment due process. The district court upheld the procedure and granted summary judgment to DiGiovanni.

A divided Second Circuit reversed in Judge Pratt’s opinion, Pinsky v. Duncan. It understood Sniadach and the later prejudgment-remedy cases to permit postponing a hearing only for exceptional circumstances supported by additional safeguards. Unlike Mitchell’s documentary payment dispute, this assault claim depended on disputed events in a fight that a judge could not reliably assess from the plaintiff alone. Judge Pratt also considered the missing bond independently defective, expressly as his own view.

At the appellate court’s invitation, Connecticut intervened after oral argument under 28 U.S.C. § 2403(b) to defend its statute’s constitutionality. Connecticut and DiGiovanni petitioned for Supreme Court review. The Supreme Court heard argument on January 7, 1991; its task concerned this use of the statute, not the merits of the assault action.

sections.title: The Supreme Court weighs the homeowner’s interest and error risk
sections.cue: Why did leaving Doehr in possession still require due process?
paragraphs: Justice White placed the case in the line of Sniadach, Fuentes, Mitchell and North Georgia Finishing and adapted the Mathews v. Eldridge framework to a private party’s use of state power. The first factor was the affected private interest; the second was the risk of error and value of further safeguards; the third focused principally on the claimant’s interest in obtaining the remedy, with attention to ancillary governmental interests and administrative burdens.

An attachment did not physically dispossess Doehr and was less severe than losing household goods or wages. It nevertheless clouded title, impaired sale or transfer, affected credit, reduced access to a home-equity loan or additional mortgage, and could trigger an insecurity clause in an existing mortgage. Due process protects temporary and partial property impairments as well as complete physical losses.

The attachment assumed a future damages award that might never occur. Connecticut’s probable-cause standard was obscure: the State initially described an objective likelihood of success, Doehr understood a subjective good-faith belief, and the State’s oral argument likened it to a complaint surviving dismissal. A facially valid allegation or sincere belief could support attachment despite defenses, jury rejection, or even failure to state a claim under the weakest understanding. Even an objective-success standard could not make the skeletal, one-sided affidavit reliable. A fight does not ordinarily lend itself to the straightforward documents found in a debt or delinquent-payment case.

An expeditious later hearing, notice, review of an adverse decision and a double-damages action for a suit lacking probable cause did not adequately correct that initial risk. Mitchell had similar protections but also a vendor’s lien, documentary issues and a bond. A later finding that probable cause was absent could not undo the deprivation that an earlier hearing could have prevented.

sections.title: No demonstrated urgency justified acting without Doehr
sections.cue: What distinguished this claimant from someone protecting an existing interest or preventing dissipation?
paragraphs: DiGiovanni had no existing stake in the home, only an interest in collecting a possible judgment. He did not allege that Doehr was about to transfer or encumber it or otherwise make it unavailable. A properly supported allegation of that kind could supply exigent circumstances for postponing the hearing, but it was absent here.

The State’s interest did not exceed the claimant’s in these circumstances. Connecticut could not justify delay through administrative burden when its procedure already offered an immediate post-deprivation hearing. The balance therefore required advance process for this attachment.

History and contemporary practice reinforced that conclusion. Traditional attachment generally addressed threatened uncollectibility, involved creditors and required security. Nearly every state in the Court’s survey required an advance hearing, exigency, or both. The appendix described then-existing statutes; the Court did not pronounce each surveyed statute or exigency rule constitutional.

All nine Justices agreed that this attachment procedure, as applied to the unrelated tort claim without a property interest or supported urgency, violated due process. The holding left room for a different balance where a plaintiff had a pre-existing interest, reliable documentary proof, or evidence of imminent dissipation.

sections.title: Four Justices would also require a bond
sections.cue: Why must the security discussion be separated from the Court’s holding?
paragraphs: In Part IV, White, Marshall, Stevens and O’Connor would additionally require a bond or other security even when a hearing or exigency justified attachment. A hearing predicts who will prevail; it does not eliminate error. Exigency might also turn out not to exist. Security would protect against some resulting loss.

The plurality considered Connecticut’s double-damages remedy inadequate. If probable cause meant good faith or facial adequacy, recovery could require something approaching fraud, malice or a complaint that failed to state a claim. Even assuming ultimate defeat permitted recovery, the plurality identified delay, loss of the remedy following settlement, an advice-of-counsel defense and uncertainty about the original plaintiff’s ability to pay. These were alternative objections, not a definitive holding that fraud or malice was invariably necessary.

Conversely, a bond could not replace a required hearing. Money paid later might not repair a lost sale, a missed education loan or a mortgage in technical default. This bond reasoning had four votes. Parts IV and V lacked a majority even though all nine Justices agreed on the disposition stated in Part V: affirmance of the Court of Appeals and remand.

sources.pinpoint: Reasoning: Part IV; Citation; Judgment; 501 U.S. 18–24 & n.8

sections.title: The concurrences explain the decision’s limits
sections.cue: What did Rehnquist and Scalia accept, and what did they reserve?
paragraphs: Chief Justice Rehnquist, joined by Justice Blackmun, joined Parts I–III and the judgment. He emphasized that earlier cases involved personal property physically seized from its owner, while Connecticut created an incipient lien and left Doehr in possession. Extending protection to this substantial impairment broke new ground, but he agreed with it. Mechanics’ liens for incorporated labor or materials and lis pendens asserting an interest in the property being litigated involved different property connections. His distinctions were not categorical immunity for every lien or recorded notice.

Rehnquist declined to decide hypothetical bond and exigency questions. A generic bond rule also said little without specifying the amount, conditions and liability trigger. Justice Scalia joined Parts I and III and the judgment. Because this attachment was not a procedure recognized at common law, he agreed it should be tested under Mathews and failed that test. His concurrence is omitted from the assigned casebook excerpt. The modified-Mathews discussion in Part II had eight votes; Scalia did not join that part.

The Court issued its unanimous judgment on June 6, 1991. Later assigned comparisons remain separate: Shaumyan upheld the same statute in a contractor’s documentary payment dispute involving incorporated labor and materials, and Diaz rejected as-applied and consequently facial challenges to New York lis pendens under the Doehr framework. Those later applications illustrate why the particular property connection and safeguards matter; they are not additional holdings of Doehr or a present-law certification.
